characterList.description: A middle-aged man with thinning, grey hair and a blue shirt. He appears to be in his 60s or 70s.
characterList.name: James Le Fanu

content_metadata.description: This interview with James Le Fanu, a GP and medical journalist, explores the pervasive issues of overdiagnosis and overtreatment in modern medicine. Through personal anecdotes, case studies, and historical examples, Le Fanu criticizes current medical practices and calls for increased patient agency and awareness.

qAndA.answer: The phrase is 'getting your feet stuck in the piano wire,' which metaphorically represents the difficulty in disentangling from overdiagnosis and overtreatment without causing harm.
qAndA.question: What is the Norwegian phrase James Le Fanu mentions, and what does it metaphorically represent in healthcare?

qAndA.answer: He discusses a study in his practice where 40% of women over 80 were taking statins unnecessarily.
qAndA.question: What case study does James Le Fanu use to illustrate overtreatment?

qAndA.answer: He criticizes the advice of prolonged bed rest after a heart attack, which was prevalent in the 1930s. The bombing of London during World War II forced doctors to shorten bed rest due to limited hospital beds, revealing its negative consequences.
qAndA.question: What historical medical advice does James Le Fanu criticize, and what event ultimately led to its correction?

qAndA.answer: He attributes it to over-reliance on mathematical algorithms and guidelines, which doctors often blindly follow without understanding their limitations or considering individual patient needs.
qAndA.question: What does James Le Fanu believe is the primary driver of overdiagnosis and overtreatment?

qAndA.answer: While generally concerned and critical of overdiagnosis and overtreatment, James Le Fanu intersperses humor throughout his discussion, making it both engaging and thought-provoking. He seems frustrated with the current state of healthcare but optimistic that change is possible through patient awareness and doctor accountability.

text_to_speech: My name is James Le Fanu I’ve been in General Practice for 20 years, I write a regular medical column for The Daily Telegraph once a week The only way out of this is what I called the patient’s revolt. People have just got to stop believing, it’s just, you know they just have to go to their doctor, you know, and actually that’s a more direct way than say why am I taking all these pills? What’s going on here? And so that’s the first one, I mean that’s where I see it coming to a halt. I don’t see because the problem is that there’s so many guidelines, there’s so many nice this and that and all that sort of thing, nobody’s going to turn around and say, well, I sure think that we made a mistake about this and you know, I hope that we don’t think that everybody over the age of 32 should be on statins. There’s a very good Norwegian phrase for it, which is getting your feet stuck in the piano wire and the trouble is you can’t disentangle your feet from the piano wire without making a noise and you can’t disentangle us from the problems of overdiagnosis and overtreatment without making a noise. This is a really interesting phenomenon that this problem, what I call systemic or systematic iatrogenesis as opposed to you’ve give somebody a pill, and he has some awful side effect from it that’s it. Systematic is when it is as it were part of mainstream practice and of course the damage which comes from that is vastly greater than the individual doctor making a mistake or prescribing a wrong drug My real insight is that, I write this medical column for The Daily Telegraph once a week, comes out every Monday and I get some enormous correspondence, people write and tell me the story of their lives and very interesting enough too and the great and recurring theme the last ten years has been about being over treated for illnesses that they don't have and the consequences And of course it's a fascinating insight because actually this is an almost unique resource, because, you know, you hear doctors opinions and you hear critics opinions, but actually the, you know, the people who are experiencing it, you know, they are, you know, relatively unheard of, you know, at least their voice is relatively silent I actually I did a little audit of women over eighty in our practice. Forty percent of whom were taking statins. You know absolutely preposterous and then when you went through their notes, it was really interesting. They were complaining about things which nobody really taken any notice of. They were complaining about taking too many pills, they were complaining about taking too many pills they were complaining about side effects, symptoms and side effects related to their polypharmacy and all that sort of thing and nobody taken any notice of it. And this is a really good practice. You know the point is that unless one starts from the principal of understanding why it is that you shouldn't be giving statins to people over the age of seventy-five unless you realise that, you know, it is a default position. You have to have a really really good reason to prescribe it. Then you are not going to prescribe and you are going to have all these problems The whole point about mass medicalisation and particularly preventiveness is that it is not based on a knowledge base of which they have any personal direct experience, you know and indeed, you know, they can’t have any experience because I would doubt there’s a single doctor in the country who is not medically, statistically trained who understands the mathematical algorithms to which these things are based, of course it’s quantitated then therefore, it must be true it is this delusion that, you know, that you believe that only statistically-based knowledge is reliable and so on and you know, my experience is that statistically-based knowledge is not reliable. A classic example of that is the 2008 crash, you know, that was based on a mathematical algorithm of which everybody knew couldn’t possibly be true that you can sell people bum mortgages and somehow repackage them and sell them on but you know, it was mathematically demonstrable and you know, those are math algorithm, and you can force and as a result, you know, the American economy lost a trillion dollars Classic example of this was and it's from some time ago but was advised that after you had a coronary you should be in bed for six weeks to allow the muscle to heal. The heart muscle to heal and this advice was promulgated in 1930's and it was so self evident that everyone used to believe in it. Even though the patients were sitting in their beds for six weeks, you know becoming very dispirited, developing bed sores, becoming constipated, getting out of bed and falling over, having pulmonary emboli and dying, you know it was so manifestly, you know, it had so many, many adverse effects. Until in the Second World War when there were the bombing of London, the Blitz. There was an incredible demand on hospital beds, because everybody had to go somewhere. And one of the physicians said, well you know, we got to put these patients somewhere, you know let’s change this from you don't have to have six weeks of bed rest to two weeks bed rest. And all these problems started to, you know, before their eyes started evaporating. They didn't get bed sores, they didn't get pulmonary emboli, and so on and so on. And the really fascinating thing about that is that it was so the reason for the recommendation and of course the consequences I mean goodness knows what the mortality rate must have been from, you know, of prolonged bed rest. That despite the amazing adverse consequences nonetheless everybody thought they were doing the right thing and it was self evident in the case. And the comparison with this current situation with polypharmacy and overdiagnosis is you know is absolutely manifest. Everybody thinks they are doing a good thing, prescribing all these pills, stopping all these people getting strokes and heart attacks, theoretically. On the basis of obscure mathematical algorithms that they don't understand. They totally don't see the fact before their eyes that their patients are having all these adverse effects and that this is completely intolerable that you should, you know, be taking eight pills a day. Eight different medications a day and so on and so. And it's really fascinating thing about is the sense of perception and what it is and how difficult it is to change that, you know, and what changed it for bed rest was the Blitz and you know, one feels that somehow there are similar a monumental catastrophe is going to happen in order to change it for, you know, change the situation away from mass medicalisation
